# Probabilities: can you trust the number? {#sec-ch02}

A decision model gives you a number, such as "this alert is 70% likely to be an attack". As an engineer, you do not need probability theory to use that number. You need to know three practical things: what the number promises, one trap to avoid, and how to check that the number can be trusted before you build on it.

::: {.goals}
- Know what "70% likely" promises, and the rare-event trap.
- Check a model's numbers on your own past cases.
- Know why the numbers go wrong, and how they are fixed.
:::

## What "70%" promises

If the weather app says "70% chance of rain" and it does not rain, the app was not wrong. The promise is about many days: of all the days it says 70%, it should rain on about 70 out of 100.

A model's number is the same kind of promise. Among all the alerts it calls "70% likely", about 70 in 100 should turn out to be real attacks. One alert cannot prove the model right or wrong; only many alerts can.

The simplest model that gives such a number is called **logistic regression**. It works like a credit score: it adds some points for each clue (a bad threat score, a login at 3 a.m., a new country) and turns the total into a probability. Banks and hospitals have used it for decades, and we will meet it again in later chapters.

::: {.keyidea}
**A probability is checked over many cases, not one.** "70% chance of rain" means that on 100 such days, it should rain on about 70. If it does not rain tomorrow, the forecast was not wrong.
:::

## The rare-event trap

Suppose an alarm catches 99% of real attacks, but also goes off by mistake for 5% of normal activity, and real attacks are rare: 1 in 1,000 events. When the alarm goes off, what is the chance of a real attack? Most people say 95%. The answer is about **2%**.

Count it out with one lakh (100,000) events. Only 100 are attacks, and the alarm catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also set it off: 4,995 false alarms. So out of 5,094 alarms, only 99 are real.

How common something is before you look at any clue is called the **base rate**. When the base rate is low, most alarms are false, and "accuracy" becomes misleading: in our example company, a rule that *never* raises any alarm is {{< num ch02 always_benign_acc pct >}} accurate, simply because most alerts are harmless. So for rare events, ask two better questions: *of the real attacks, how many did it catch?* and *of its alarms, how many were real?*

::: {.keyidea}
**When something is rare, most alarms are false.** If only 1 in 1,000 events is an attack, even a 99%-accurate alarm is right only about 2 times in 100. To see this, count it out with 1,00,000 cases instead of using percentages.
:::

## Check the numbers before you trust them

When a model's numbers keep their promise, the model is called **calibrated**. Nothing forces a model to be calibrated, so you check it, the same way you would check the weather app:

1. Take a few hundred past cases where you already know the answer.
2. Put them in groups by what the model said: 0–10%, 10–20%, and so on.
3. In each group, count how often the event really happened.

If the model said about 70% for a group and about 70% really happened, good. @fig-forecasters shows the result as a chart: points on the diagonal line mean the numbers can be trusted; points below it mean the model is too sure of itself. People often sum up this chart in one number, the **ECE**: the average gap between what the model said and what really happened. Smaller is better.

![Two forecasters. For each thing they said ("30%", "70%" and so on), we count how often it actually happened. The careful forecaster sits on the diagonal: their 70% happens about 70% of the time. The overconfident one says 90% about things that happen only about 70% of the time.](/figures/ch04/forecasters.pdf){#fig-forecasters}

::: {.keyidea}
**A model's "80%" must really mean 80%.** Take all the cases where it said 80%: about 80 out of 100 should turn out true. This is called being calibrated. If its 80% really means 50%, every decision based on it goes wrong.
:::

Be careful not to mix this up with **ranking**: whether the model puts the most dangerous cases at the top of the list. Ranking is measured by a score called **AUC** (1 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin toss). A model can rank well and still give wrong numbers, like a teacher who orders the students correctly but writes everyone's marks 30 points too high. If you only use the order, ranking is enough. If you draw a line on the numbers, as the rest of this book does, the numbers must be right too.

## Why the numbers go wrong, and the fix

Three things commonly spoil a model's numbers:

- **A made-up 50/50 training mix.** Attacks are only {{< num ch04 base pct >}} of alerts, so someone trains the model on equal numbers of attacks and normal alerts. The model then believes attacks are common, and its numbers come out far too high.
- **Big, over-trained models** become too sure of themselves.
- **The world changes**, so last month's correct numbers can be wrong today.

The fix is usually simple and does not need retraining. Keep aside a few hundred past cases the model never trained on, and learn a small correction on top of it. The usual correction is called **Platt scaling**; another, **temperature scaling**, only tones down numbers that are too extreme. In our example, Platt scaling brought the 50/50 model's error (ECE) down from {{< num ch04 balanced.ece f2 >}} to {{< num ch04 fixes.Platt.ece f2 >}}.

Finally, check each group you treat differently. A model can be right for all alerts together but wrong for one group: in our example, for alerts from laptops it said {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.pred pct1 >}} when the truth was {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.actual pct1 >}}, and real attacks on laptops were closed without anyone looking.

::: {.keyidea}
**A model that is right on average can still be wrong for one group.** It may be correct for all alerts together but wrong for laptop alerts, or for one language or one region. Check each group separately.
:::

::: {.breaks}
A model whose numbers were correct last month may not be correct today, because the world changes: new kinds of attacks, new software, new users. And correct numbers do not make every single answer right: if the model honestly says 70%, it will still be wrong about three times out of ten. So keep checking the model on recent cases, again and again.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. A spam filter catches 98% of spam and wrongly flags 1% of normal emails. If only 1% of all emails are spam, what fraction of flagged emails are actually normal? Count it out with 10,000 emails.
:::

Next chapter: now that we have numbers we can trust, where should we draw the line between "act" and "ignore"?
:::
